A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 18 pages of each, including equations, figures, tables, code, and appendices A–E, support reliable comparison despite reordering.

before.justification: v2 reports original Monte Carlo simulations, distribution-shift experiments, and Chatbot Arena evaluations, including additional simulation results in the appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains these original simulations and Chatbot Arena evaluations in Sections 7–8 and the appendices.

M1.justification: Equations (4)–(8), Algorithm 1, and Appendix C retain the same estimator, confidence interval, and pilot-based calibration allocation. The supplied Python code is identical; changing 'bias-adjusted' to 'bias-corrected' does not change the procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same binary simulation tasks, label-shift scenarios, and Chatbot Arena win-rate task with the same six target models. The additional online-test-data discussion introduces no evaluated scenario.

E2.justification: The naive-estimator and equal-allocation comparisons remain unchanged. The distribution-shift comparison retains the same five estimators: naive, calibration-only, difference/PPI, conditional calibration, and the proposed misclassification-adjusted estimator. Chen et al. (2026) is cited but not newly evaluated.

E3.justification: Main simulations retain n = 1000, m = 200, and 21 true-accuracy settings; appendix simulations retain the same judge parameters and m = 200 or 500. Chatbot Arena still uses GPT-4.1-mini and 90%/10% test/calibration splits. Caption corrections do not establish a changed experimental procedure.

E4.justification: The equal-versus-adaptive allocation analysis, sensitivity to calibration size and judge reliability, and distribution-shift bias analysis are retained. Their relocation between sections and appendices adds no new robustness or supplementary analysis.

E5.justification: Both report 10,000 Monte Carlo replications, 100 random Chatbot Arena splits, and the same 95% confidence-interval reporting practice. The new probability bound concerns a theoretical proposition, not a changed empirical uncertainty procedure.

E6.justification: The Chatbot Arena table is identical after renumbering from v2 Table 2 to v3 Table 1, including Alpaca coverage 96% with interval length 0.193 and GPT-4 coverage 97% with length 0.210. Matched simulation, distribution-shift, and Arena bias plots retain their values and trends, including appendix Figures 9–16.

T1.justification: Proposition 6.1 gains a Hoeffding-based probability-qualified sufficient condition for finite calibration size; the earlier necessary-and-sufficient criterion is retained only as m approaches infinity. Conversely, v2's allocation-optimality proof in Proposition B.2 disappears although main-text Proposition 5.2 remains. Section 3 also changes the main assumption to P = Q, treating label shift separately in Section 8.

C1.justification: The introduction removes v2's assertion that prior LLM-judge discussions offered no method for valid intervals. The conclusion narrows calibration design from being preferable to increasing judgments to being an effective strategy. The central estimator, uncertainty-quantification, human-evaluation comparison, and distribution-shift contributions remain.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly acknowledges that its estimator may have higher variance than alternatives and uses this tradeoff to motivate adaptive allocation. Section 6 newly explains that human-only estimation variance arises from sampling instances, while Section 8 adds a fixed-calibration versus changing-test-data explanation for label shift. Existing future-work limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C retains identical implementation code and the same repository-access statement. The pilot-size example and experimental details are unchanged or relocated between Appendices D and E; no substantive reproducibility information is added or removed.

R1.justification: v3 adds Chen et al. (2026) and more explicitly acknowledges lower-variance alternatives while motivating its choice through distribution-shift robustness. The classical calibration and PPI foundations remain; other reference changes are predominantly bibliographic.

P1.justification: Extensive rewriting spans the abstract and most main-text sections. Contributions are reorganized, Sections 7–8 and Appendices D–E exchange order, and method subsections become numbered. Terminology and the impact statement are revised, acknowledgments are added, and two erroneous 'Appendix 9' references are introduced.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 2b are redrawn or relabeled, and Figure 4 and the Arena bias plot receive clearer labels or captions. Existing figures and tables move with the reordered sections. The Monte Carlo caption corrects its equal-allocation panel reference from (a,c) to (a,b), without adding plots or changing their results.

improvement.justification: The revised Proposition 6.1 makes calibration-sample uncertainty more explicit, and v3 better explains sampling variance and competing estimators' advantages. However, it removes the proof supporting the retained allocation-optimality claim and introduces erroneous 'Appendix 9' references. With empirical evidence unchanged, these gains and losses in theoretical completeness leave the net quality direction uncertain.
